Anaemia in Peruvian children aged 6-59 months

Dataset 6: Peru DHS child anaemia and growth extract

RSR feasibility analysis

2026-08-03

Introduction

Childhood anaemia is Peru’s most prevalent nutritional condition: roughly four in ten children aged 6-59 months fall below the 11 g/dL altitude-adjusted haemoglobin threshold, and national reduction targets have been repeatedly missed. The Peruvian Demographic and Health Survey (ENDES) measures haemoglobin in every surveyed child of this age and links it to household wealth, maternal characteristics, geography and water and sanitation conditions, which is the data structure used in published ENDES analyses of the determinants of childhood anaemia (for example Gonzales and colleagues on anaemia and altitude in Peruvian children).

Aim. Among Peruvian children aged 6-59 months, we examined which of child age, child sex, natural region, household wealth, maternal education, maternal indigenous identity and household water source are independently associated with anaemia, mutually adjusting for the others.

This is a Purpose 3 analysis: several predictors are of interest and the question is which remain associated with the outcome after mutual adjustment.

Methods

Data source. A cross-sectional extract of 19191 children aged 6-59 months from the Peru Demographic and Health Survey (ENDES), a nationally implemented household survey, each linked to their mother’s interview and household record.

Variables. The outcome is anaemia, a binary indicator defined as altitude-adjusted haemoglobin below 11 g/dL; the modelled event is anaemia = Yes. Predictors are child age in months (continuous, 6-59); child sex (reference Female); natural region (reference Lima metropolitan); household wealth quintile (reference Poorest); mother’s highest education (reference Primary or none); maternal indigenous identity (reference No); and an unimproved household water source (reference No, i.e. improved source). These seven cover child biology, geography, household socio-economic position and the environmental route to anaemia through waterborne infection and parasitism.

haemoglobin_g_dl is excluded by construction: anaemia is exactly haemoglobin_g_dl < 11, so including it would produce a deterministic, perfectly separating model. Height-for-age and stunting are also excluded because they are co-outcomes of undernutrition rather than exposures. survey_weight is never a predictor.

Statistical analysis. Logistic regression via glm(family = binomial), justified because the outcome is binary; estimates are reported as odds ratios. We fitted a univariable model for each predictor first, then a single multivariable model containing all of them. Predictors were chosen in advance on subject-matter grounds, not by significance. Significance threshold 0.05; estimates are reported with 95% confidence intervals. Assumptions were checked with performance::check_model(). Analysis used R version 4.6.0 (2026-04-24) with tidyverse, gtsummary and performance.

Missing data. Complete-case analysis: 19039 of 19191 rows were analysed (152 dropped, 0.8%). The only predictor with appreciable missingness is the water-source variable.

36.2% of children (6895 of 19039) were anaemic. Anaemic children are markedly younger (median 23 versus 37 months) and are over-represented in the poorest quintiles, in the highlands and jungle, and in indigenous households.

Figure 1. Prevalence of anaemia by household wealth quintile and natural region.

Anaemia prevalence falls steadily across wealth quintiles within every region, and the highlands and jungle sit above Lima and the rest of the coast at almost every level of wealth, so the two gradients are partly independent of each other.

Child age dominates: each additional month of age is associated with 3.8% lower odds of anaemia (OR 0.962, 95% CI 0.96 to 0.964, p < 0.001), which compounds to roughly a 0.63-fold change in odds per year of life. Among the categorical predictors, maternal indigenous identity (OR 1.98), an unimproved water source (OR 1.82) and highland residence (OR 2.02) all roughly double the crude odds, while the richest quintile has about 70% lower odds than the poorest. Child sex is the only predictor that does not reach significance (OR 1.06, p = 0.054).

Why adjustment is needed

The crude odds ratios above are not comparable to each other because the exposures overlap heavily. Child age confounds nearly everything: anaemia prevalence falls from about two thirds in infancy to under a quarter at four years, and the age distribution differs across regions and wealth quintiles, so any crude social contrast partly compares younger with older children. Household wealth confounds both the water-source and the indigenous contrasts: unimproved water supply and indigenous ethnicity are both concentrated in the poorest quintiles, and poverty independently affects diet quality, supplementation uptake and infection burden, so the crude OR of 1.82 for unimproved water is partly a poverty estimate. Natural region confounds the wealth gradient in turn, since the highlands and jungle are simultaneously poorer and, for the highlands, higher-altitude with a residual altitude effect that the haemoglobin adjustment formula may not fully remove. Mutual adjustment is needed before any of these can be described as independent.

The model has AIC 2.24925^{4} with 14 parameters and 6895 events, giving 530.4 events per parameter – far above the conventional minimum of 10, so the model is comfortably identified and there is no need to reduce the predictor set. Conditional on the other six predictors, each additional month of age is associated with 3.9% lower odds of anaemia (OR 0.961, 95% CI 0.959 to 0.963). Highland residence carries 1.51 times the odds of anaemia relative to Lima (95% CI 1.34 to 1.7) and the jungle 1.5 times, at the same age, sex, wealth, education, ethnicity and water source. The wealth gradient remains monotonic: the richest quintile has 53% lower adjusted odds than the poorest. An unimproved water source retains an adjusted OR of 1.36 (95% CI 1.19 to 1.54), and maternal indigenous identity 1.25.

Several odds ratios move sharply toward the null. Maternal indigenous identity falls from OR 1.98 crude to 1.25 adjusted, and unimproved water from 1.82 to 1.36: in both cases roughly half the crude excess odds was wealth, region and education, and only a modest independent association remains. The richest-versus-poorest contrast also attenuates, from OR 0.3 to 0.47. By contrast child age barely moves at all (OR 0.962 crude to 0.961 adjusted), because age is essentially unrelated to the social and environmental covariates – the textbook picture of a predictor that needs no adjustment. Two coefficients change interpretation entirely. Higher maternal education is strongly protective crudely (OR 0.58, p < 0.001) but is null after adjustment (OR 0.95, p = 0.39); and secondary education actually flips direction, from OR 0.89 (protective, p = 0.003) to 1.1 (p = 0.037). Maternal education is so tightly bound to wealth and region that once those are held constant it carries essentially no independent information about anaemia, and the small residual reversal should not be over-interpreted. The highlands coefficient is the interesting exception in the opposite direction: it attenuates only modestly, from 2.02 to 1.51, so the highland excess is not simply poverty.

Diagnostics

For a logistic model the relevant panels are the following. Binned residuals: 64.5% of bins fall inside the error bounds; the standard rule of thumb is that about 95% should, so this model shows a real, if modest, lack of fit. The pattern is driven by the linear age term – anaemia prevalence falls steeply from 6 to 24 months and then flattens, which a single log-odds slope cannot follow – and a spline or age-group factor would fix it. Collinearity is low throughout (maximum VIF 1.97), so despite the strong pairwise associations between wealth, education, region and ethnicity the adjusted odds ratios are estimated stably; the education reversal noted above is a substantive confounding result and not a variance-inflation artefact. Influential observations show no points outside the Cook’s distance contours, which is expected with 19039 rows. Events per parameter is 530.4, so overfitting and sparse-data bias are not concerns. Homogeneity of variance and normality of residuals are printed by check_model() for completeness but do not apply to a binomial GLM.

Discussion

Anaemia in Peruvian preschool children is overwhelmingly a condition of the second year of life: adjusted odds fall by about 3.9% per month of age, so an 8-month-old has several times the odds of a 4-year-old in the same household. On top of that age effect sit a clear wealth gradient and a substantial highland and jungle excess that survives adjustment for wealth, education and ethnicity. Water source contributes an independent but smaller amount. Practically, this supports concentrating iron supplementation and screening on infants and one-year-olds, with geographic targeting of the highlands and jungle rather than socio-economic targeting alone.

Limitations. Cross-sectional design: haemoglobin, water source and household wealth are all measured at the same visit, so no temporal ordering is established and no causal claim is warranted. The outcome is a dichotomised version of a continuous measurement, which discards information and makes results sensitive to the 11 g/dL cut-point and to the altitude-adjustment formula; children in the highlands sit near the cut-point in large numbers, so misclassification is non-random with respect to a key predictor. The source ENDES analysis used the DHS complex design – cluster (HV001), stratum (HV022) and sampling weights – whereas this extract contains only the weight, which is deliberately not used here; standard errors are therefore too narrow, estimates are not design-corrected, and this sample must not be described as nationally representative. With 19039 rows almost everything is statistically significant, so interpretation must lead with effect sizes: the sex difference, for example, is significant in neither model and would be irrelevant even if it were. Major determinants are simply absent: iron supplementation, recent infection, dietary diversity, maternal anaemia, helminth infection and exact altitude of residence. Finally, the binned-residual check shows the linear age term does not fit well, so the age odds ratio should be read as an average slope rather than a constant effect.

Future work. Refit with the DHS survey design and a spline or age-group factor for child age, and if possible model haemoglobin continuously rather than dichotomised.

Feasibility notes

Not part of a student report.

  • Works, with one large caveat. 6895 events, 530.4 events per parameter, no separation, no sparse cells, maximum VIF 1.97. Statistically this is a safe logistic exercise.
  • FATAL trap: the deterministic twin. anaemia is exactly haemoglobin_g_dl < 11. A student who puts haemoglobin in the model gets perfect separation and either an error or absurd odds ratios. This must be called out explicitly in the brief for this dataset; it is the single most likely way for a student to destroy this analysis.
  • Redundant with the haemoglobin outcome. This is the same research question as haemoglobin_g_dl, run on a thrown-away version of the same measurement. It is a fine logistic-regression exercise, but a student should be told to do one or the other, not both, and that the continuous version is the better analysis.
  • Binned residuals fail (64.5% within bounds). Caused by the non-linear age effect. Good teaching material, but students will need help reading the panel and will otherwise report “diagnostics fine”.
  • Education sign flip. Secondary education reverses direction between crude and adjusted models. It is real confounding, not collinearity (VIF 1.97), but it will confuse students and needs supervision.
  • Sample size. At 19039 rows everything is significant; the brief must force effect-size-led interpretation.
  • Design not honoured. Only the weight is present, not cluster or stratum, so a design-correct analysis is impossible from this extract.
